Overcoming a Child's Resistance to Late Adoption: How One New Attachment can Facilitate Another

Juliet Hopkins

Juliet Hopkins

London
57 Woodsome Road
London NW5 1SA

Juliet Hopkins   Child and adult psychotherapist who has an honorary position at the Tavistock Clinic following her retirement from the staff in December 1999. She is a tutor on the BAP Child Psychotherapy Training. Her special interest is in early child development and parent-infant psychotherapy. She is in private practice with adults and young families.
Adoption; Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD); attachment; disorganized attachment; loyalty conflict.

The paper describes the difficulty which late-adopted children may have in forming attachments to their new parents. It considers the nature of the disorganized attachment pattern which many of these deprived, abused children display and the origin of this pattern in experiences of ‘fright without solution’.

The psychotherapy of a 9-year-old, late-adopted boy is used to illustrate long-standing resistance to new attachments on account of defences on which security depends, and the persistence of loyalty to prior internal attachment representations. Change becomes possible through psychotherapy in which earlier negative attachment models are externalized together with their associated feelings of ‘fright without solution’. For this boy, a long period of rejection of the therapist gave way to a new capacity to play together; this was associated with the development of positive attachments to the boy's adoptive parents.

Preventive Work in a Toddler Group and Nursery

Marie Zaphiriou

Marie Zaphiriou

London
21 Hillfield Road
London NW6 1QD

Marie Zaphiriou   Child and adult analyst, working in private practice and as a member of staff at the Anna Freud Centre. She was the psychoanalytic consultant to the Anna Freud Nursery from 1986 to 1997, and is currently consultant for the expanding Toddler Group service. She is involved in the supervision and teaching of child psychotherapy trainees at the Anna Freud Centre.
Young children; toddler group; nursery; parent guidance; preventive work; fathers.

This paper is about the sort of preventive work which can be carried out in early child care settings where incipient disturbance can be picked up and worked with promptly and effectively. It shows how toddler groups and nurseries can offer relationships and experiences which encourage mutuality and progressive development, while at the same time addressing difficulties before they have become fully internalized. It gives a detailed account of work with a single mother and her son who attended first a toddler group run by a child psychotherapist and her trainee assistant, and then a nursery where staff were in regular consultation with the child psychotherapist who also worked individually with the mother. It argues that the effectiveness of such early interventions can be conceptualized in terms of supplying maternal and paternal functioning at a time when children and parents alike are particularly needful of and responsive to this sort of help.

Editorial

Judith Edwards and Mary Walker

Mary Walker

Mary Walker  

With the opening of the third millennium, in Volume 26 Number 1 of the Journal, we are pleased to present a spectrum of papers which both link with past concerns and address those which will continue to preoccupy us as a profession as we embark on our fifty-first year of practice.

We begin with a timely paper on the origins of violence in the psyche: ‘Broken links’ by Suzanne Maiello from Rome. In her paper the author takes up a debate which is also at the forefront of public concern. By linking her own and a supervisee's work with contemporary events in Italy, she offers further thinking on the important differences between ‘aggression’ which is essentially an object-related emotion, and ‘destruction’, where notions of linking have either been destroyed or never existed. This results in a dissociated mindless state where the loss of the object engenders states which are incomprehensible, incommunicable and inaccessible.

We inaugurated the correspondence section of the Journal (Vol. 22 No. 1 1996) with Robert Furman's letter about the prescription of Ritalin in the States and his concerns about what appeared to be its over-use as a solution to difficulties with children diagnosed as having attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Further correspondence ensued (Vol. 22 No. 2 1996) and also two papers on the subject (Vol. 24 No. 2 1998). We are pleased to continue the debate in this issue with the publication of Maria Pozzi's paper ‘Ritalin for whom?’, in which, through her work with two families of children under 5 in London where the Ritalin option had been offered, she and the families struggle with the internal dynamics which are often externalized as a tension between psychological and pharmacological approaches. As she observes, short-term psychodynamic family counselling of the kind she describes has great value in a climate of financial restrictions.

Bob Hinshelwood  

Dear Editors,

Thank you for asking me to write about the practice of child psychotherapy in Sweden, with reference to Alan Shuttleworth's paper ‘Finding new clinical pathways in the changing world of district child psychotherapy’ in the Journal of Child Psychotherapy (April 1999 25(1)).

I read the paper with great interest. It gave an overview of the situation in the UK with its complexities, it shed light on the present situation in Sweden and gave me inspiration to think about future development in the work in district clinics and for child psychotherapists in Sweden.

In Sweden there are, as in the UK, geographically based child and adolescent psychiatry service teams. In Stockholm they are called child and adolescent mental health services, and in the rest of the country, child and adolescent psychiatry clinics. I will refer to them all as district clinics, as Alan Shuttleworth does. In the Stockholm area there are thirty district clinics serving a population of 420,000 children and adolescents, up to the age of 19.

In Sweden we face many similar problems to our colleagues in the UK. We also have the very difficult situation of an increasing demand for help from families. In Stockholm there has been a 70 per cent increase in the last six years, without any corresponding increase in resources. The development is similar in the rest of the country, and is probably due to cut-backs in schools and other public services. There is a political demand, at least within the Stockholm County Council area, that district clinics are not to operate waiting lists. Families are not to wait for more than three weeks for at least a first consultation session. This creates great pressure on the clinics and the clinic staff. Preventing therapist overwork and ‘burn out’ is a huge problem.

The Legacy of Abuse by his Mother for a 10-Year-Old Boy

Suzanne Beech

Suzanne Beech

Stourbridge
51 Sweetpool Lane
West Hagley
Stourbridge DY8 2XA

Suzanne Beech   Worked as a social worker for eighteen years before training as a child psychotherapist with the Birmingham Trust for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. She is particularly interested in working with children who have been subject to abuse or neglect, and currently works for Midland Foster Care Associates, an independent fostering organization which provides packages of care, support and therapy for such children.
Early abuse, mother/son abuse, pathological organization, pathological splitting, omnipotence, omniscience,

This paper seeks to explore some of the effects of abuse by a mother on her very young son. It considers how the primitive capacity for coping with anxiety by splitting and projection has been rendered ineffectual, and how the structures that have evolved to compensate have profoundly affected the boy's emotional and mental capacities. In the first fifteen months of therapy, the boy has begun to make some tentative moves towards effective splitting and projection, with its hope of healthier growth. This hope is hard for him to bear, involving, as it must, searing depressive pain. There is consequently a powerful pull towards a pathological organization where omnipotence and omniscience offer, disastrously, an exciting and pain-free alternative. The boy's therapy and his therapist are exposed to the full impact of the omnipotent onslaught, and evolving ways of bearing this and continuing to think was not only essential for survival but, also, a major tool of the therapy.

Roger Kennedy  

Christopher Bollas's new book is to be highly recommended. As with his other books, this is an evocative and stimulating addition to the psychoanalytic literature, written in his unique and compelling literary style; and it continues to develop his important contributions to psychoanalytic theory and technique. The title is from the last act of King Lear, where the king is both mad and yet sees the truth of things for the first time. One of Bollas's main themes is how the psychoanalytic method of free association leads to the discovery of the patient's truth by means which completely undermine the structure of Western epistemology. The method of free association and the act of interpretation decentre the patient's usual grasp of things; and, by breaking up the customary thread of discourse, the patient's truth is approached. Like Lear, the patient in a sense has to experience a form of madness in order to see clearly. Yet Bollas emphasizes how neither Freud nor those who have come after him have found this discovery an easy one. Free association is still subversive; we still need certainties; and there is a resistance to free association. Freud released us by his method to be continuously mysterious to ourselves and others. This is not only a philosophical position but also has clinical implications. As the analytic narrative moves in puzzling ways, ‘patients become informatively incoherent and they learn that the analyst wants them to speak passing ideas occurring in the back of the mind, caught up as they are in the logic of narrative about something quite unrelated. “But if I tell you what I am thinking, I won't make sense,” is an understandable cry, yet in time they come to appreciate this remarkable and strange freedom to speak in fragments’ (pp. 1-2).

Jenny Kaplan-Davids  

Freud (1909) wrote, ‘a thing which has not been understood inevitably reappears: like an unlaid ghost, it cannot rest until the mystery has been solved and the spell broken’.

This book, another in the Tavistock Clinic Series, describes the meeting with and laying to rest of many such ghosts in the work of the Unit for the Study of Trauma and its Aftermath in the Adult Department of the Tavistock Clinic.

The book provides many detailed accounts of assessment, consultation, short- and long-term work of differing frequencies with traumatized patients. The writing is lively and clear and I found myself reading the clinical accounts with a sense of expectation.

All the chapters are written by clinicians who have been associated with the Unit's work. Throughout there is a thoughtful and thought-provoking integration of theory with practice. The writers convey the detail and the rich complexity of the therapeutic processes vividly. The diagram on page 24, which attempts to present a visual summary of the interplay of the contribution of the individual and the event, is helpful, especially as one reads on and gathers more of a sense of the different kinds of cases and experiences.

I sensed the difficult nature of this work, particularly the resistances against the symbolization and higher-level representation of traumatic experiences, and the restoration of the link with the representation of the benign object. A separate chapter on resistances would have been helpful.

There are five sections. The introduction, which comprises part one, contains a very clear exposition of the central psychoanalytic views which run through the book. As evident from the title, the book has a distinctive psychoanalytic approach to trauma and traumatic stress. The focus is placed on the treatment of traumatized states of mind. Caroline Garland traces the history of the concept of trauma through early Freud to more contemporary approaches. While acknowledging the Freudian notion of helplessness as a central component of the experience of trauma, the writers bring together theories of internal states of mind with traumatic situations. Garland clarifies the distinction Freud made between automatic anxiety and signal anxiety.

Chriso Andreou   Trained as a child psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic. She is also a founding member of Nafsiyat, Intercultural Psychotherapy Centre. Previously she was the Senior Child Psychotherapist at the adolescent community team in Wandsworth, London, and has undertaken clinical research into sexually abusive behaviour in young adolescent boys at Great Ormond Street Hospital.
Adolescence; abuse; internalization; homelessness; psychoanalytic psychotherapy; separation anxiety.

This paper describes psychotherapy with two adolescents who are in the care of the local authority. Attention is drawn to the fact that the social workers responsible for these young people can be drawn into the chaos, despair and helplessness of their client's internal states. This is linked to the therapist's struggle to think, maintain hope and sustain a structured space. Interpretations address the leading anxiety and transform repetitive acting out into communication. The paper illustrates the relationship between the compulsion to act out and the bleakness of an internal world within which there is no sustaining object, and explores the potential for a therapeutic setting to provide a structured space within which traumatic experiences can be named and thought about.

In this paper we describe research using narrative techniques to examine the effects of past abuse, and the process of subsequent recovery, in children aged 4-8. Editorial

Mary Walker and Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows  

This edition of the journal contains papers, both national and international, which detail some of the varied settings in which child psychotherapists work. It also continues our theme of describing the development of child psychotherapy in other parts of the world, and here we focus on Australia. Previously, there have been papers describing child psychotherapy in Russia and Hungary, 24(1) and Italy, 25(3); plus a recent letter (Correspondence, 25(3)) from child psychotherapists in Sydney, NSW, which outlined how the practice of child psychotherapy has been established in a very different way from that in the United Kingdom and how this poses different dilemmas for practitioners. In this edition, we are pleased to open with Frances Thomson Salo's comprehensive account of the historical context for the establishment of training in child psychotherapy in Australia and how the service is developing in ways that are culturally and geographically relevant. We would like to thank Frances Thomson Salo for all her help in encouraging her Australian colleagues to contribute to this edition and acting as our guest editor ‘down-under’.

Our first paper comes from Melbourne, Australia. In ‘The role of the body as the medium in child psychotherapy’, Marell Lynch gives a compelling account of her work with an 11-year-old girl who had been severely abused and rejected by her biological mother, followed by a succession of foster placements. She describes how the current thinking in mental health services about therapeutic work with such damaged children is to provide more responsive and briefer treatment models. This challenges the child psychotherapist to consider alternative models of intervention, involving changes in technique, role and the use of a time-limited intervention. In her work with Gina, she strove to provide a model which acknowledged the child's psychobiological experience of trauma and disrupted attachments as well as giving a voice to the child's experiences.

Frances Salo   Child and adult psychoanalyst and a member of the British and Australian Psycho-analytical Societies. She works in private practice in Melbourne, Australia and is a senior lecturer on the University of Melbourne Masters in Infant and Parent Mental Health.

The child psychotherapy scene in Australia, a continent the size of Europe with a population of 18 million, is a challenging but exciting one, with clinical work and thinking that is deeply sensitive and original at its best. Child and adolescent mental health services have developed to meet the specific needs of the Australian milieu, and there is much that is innovative. Where clinicians once worked in a climate of isolation from developments in other countries, which have a stronger tradition of child psychotherapy, now with advances in communication technology there is a greater sense of connection with developments elsewhere. The two papers in this section have been written by clinicians who work in the two largest cities, Sydney and Melbourne, and who both write with clinical experience of more than twenty years. Before discussing the papers, I will briefly set them in a historical context and outline some developments in child psychotherapy training and service development. What follows is a personal view which I hope my colleagues here will feel represents developments in the field well enough.

Historical Context

Child psychotherapy in Australia would probably be thought of as beginning in 1936 when Ruth Drake, a nursery teacher and speech therapist, was appointed to run a Child Guidance Nursery in the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, Victoria. She was subsequently appointed as the first child psychotherapist in the Department of Psychiatry of the Royal Children's Hospital.

Editorial

Mary Walker and Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows

Paul Barrows  

It is some seventeen years since the publication of the pioneering work of Boston and Szur, Psychotherapy with Severely Deprived Children (Boston and Szur, 1983). This book brought together work that had been undertaken in the Fostering and Adoption Workshop at the Tavistock Clinic. The members of this workshop wished to explore whether children from very deprived backgrounds could benefit from individual psychotherapy. Previously it had been a widely held view that such children, having very little ego strength, were not suitable candidates and needed, rather, The Provision of Primary Experience (Docker-Drysdale, 1990) that they had lacked.

The work was extremely challenging and demanding upon the resilience of the therapists, but a body of experience gradually accrued that gave hope that these children could be reached and helped, particularly if the therapist could tackle their tendency to deprive themselves further by resisting help when this did become available (see Henry, 1974). It is these children - almost by definition some of the most disturbed and disturbing - who now typically form a large part of the child psychotherapist's caseload and they remain as difficult and challenging as ever. Much creative thinking has also gone on in the interim, trying to elucidate ways of helping them (for example, Alvarez, 1992). There has been a particular emphasis in this work on how technique and interpretation may need to be modified to take account of the deficits in the early life experience of these children, who have not had much chance to ‘be a kid’ in the sense we would normally think of.

It is, therefore, a pleasure to be able to publish the papers gathered in this volume which help to illustrate the ‘state of the art’ in psychoanalytic work with this group. The first three articles, by Juliet Hopkins, Judith Edwards and Debbie Hindle, focus on clinical work with children in stable placements (either adopted or, in one case, a child returned from foster-care to live with his own father) and it is fascinating to see how certain themes recur.

This issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry is devoted to the particular child psychotherapy training and work of the Tavistock Clinic. It is a collection of papers that describe, in a concise and accessible way, different aspects of this work. Taken together, they present a coherent overview of current practice. A useful framework is provided in a paper by Margaret Rustin which describes the history, development and philosophy of the training. Dilys Daws, in her opening comments to the book, suggests that the aim was to give a live account of work in progress. The selection made by the editors does convey the sense of a contained, but lively, dynamic process which manages to draw together and interweave the different strands of the work.

As an example, the ‘Training in Infant Observation’ that has developed with the clinical training and now forms a crucial precursor to it is described briefly here by Lisa Miller. However, its value and purpose in developing a core understanding of the emotional development of infants and young children, as well as the capacity to adopt an observational stance, form an underlying current through many of the papers. For instance, in an illuminating paper on introjective processes, Gianna Williams uses material from infant observation as well as session material to draw out and illustrate the processes of the introjection of objects which can either facilitate or hinder an infant's development. The distinctions she establishes here centre around the underlying theme of the close interrelationship between maternal states of mind and an infant's emotional development and capacity for thought.

The theme of the impact of maternal states of mind on an infant is further elaborated in Judith Loose's paper, in which she describes generally the range of work child psychotherapists do with parents, but looks in particular at her brief work with two maternally deprived mothers. She looks in detail at the changes and meaning of each session as these mothers express their need for a ‘parenting experience’ for themselves, illustrating in a very direct way how a containing maternal function is central to the work of a child psychotherapist.

This book is part of a Tavistock Clinic series, some volumes of which have already been reviewed in this journal. It is presented as a tribute to the multiple contributions of Hanna Segal to the understanding of the relationship of psychoanalysis to culture in its widest sense. The extent of her work is reviewed in Bell's introduction, which in itself provides an important framework for thinking about the book as a whole.

Bell points out that, although psychoanalytic knowledge depends for its existence on psychoanalytic practice, it is not coextensive with it and, on this basis, asserts that psychoanalysis itself should thus be seen as a body of knowledge of the mind (author's emphasis) conceptually distinct from its application. In support of this view he draws on the distinction made by Freud (1926) between the scientific structure of the body of knowledge which constitutes psychoanalysis and its application in both clinical and non-clinical contexts. He also stresses the pre-eminence within the Kleinian perspective of the need to struggle to relate to the truth as emphasized by Bion (1962, 1970). In view of the above, he contends - I think successfully - that psychoanalytic knowledge can be properly used in conjunction with the arts only if it is respected as an intrinsic body of knowledge in its own right and not used as a kind of analogy or metaphor. He is also able to assert that this book should not be regarded as being concerned with ‘applied psychoanalysis’, a subject which is sometimes viewed as being more speculative than clinical work. Bell's insistence on the need for such a firm parameter in my view increases the authority and validity of the book as a whole.

The first part, under the heading ‘Art and Literature’, consists of discussions of four, generally acclaimed, pieces of literature.

Sara Klaniczay   Qualified as both a child and an adult psychoanalyst, and is a training analyst of the Hungarian Psycho-Analytic Society. She works in private practice and currently lectures at a training college for teachers of handicapped children.
Stuttering, clinging, sense of self, speech development, security,

In the treatment of stuttering I use the same therapeutic approach as with any other neurotic condition. I do not attempt to deal directly with the symptom, but try to make use of the child's repetitive play to bring the damaging experience to the surface and to understand the underlying connections. This may, in part, be interpreted to the child.

Difficulties to do with the need for an object (‘clinging’) are central. These are generally resolved spontaneously in a therapeutic relationship which offers security. Other problems, which manifest themselves in the negative transference, can be interpreted.

Where the stuttering is long established and convulsive, it is not enough to understand the underlying dynamics. The child needs also to have repeated experience of spontaneous relaxation, e.g. in the course of joyful manual activity which can become a behaviour pattern (internalized).

An important part of the therapeutic task is to deal with and relieve the anxiety of the mother. When the child has been stuttering for a time, a vicious circle can develop where the child's stuttering induces anxiety in the mother and mother's anxiety increases the child's tendency to stutter. Case histories are used to illustrate the theme.

This paper follows the progress of four years of twice-weekly psychoanalytic psychotherapy with a borderline girl aged 4 at the start of treatment. It describes how her early experience with her mother, who was ill, and her subsequent removal from her mother and placement with a foster-family led to her having severe difficulties in relating to others. Using the work of Ekstein as a framework, it follows the changes in the child's behaviour in the therapy from acting out to playing with toys to role playing to the apparent development of her capacity to phantasize. It focuses on what the dolls’ house represented for her and how it came to be a transitional space where the inner world of the child could be represented. Letter to the editors from Dr Lorne Loxterkamp

Devon, England

Dear Editors,

When I wrote my piece on Segal's idea of symbolic equation (this Journal Vol. 25 No. 3 1999: 498-502), I hoped to stimulate a debate on a topic that has suffered from frequent, sterile repetitions. I have always doubted the validity of symbolic equation (hereafter SE); and it was Segal's completely unchanged account in these pages (Vol. 24 No. 3 1998: 349-357) that prompted me to formulate a critical assessment. In their replies, Trevor Lubbe and Bob Hinshelwood try to preserve the notion, but do not succeed. Let me deal with their main points in turn.

Lubbe misrepresents my argument in several places because he hasn't read it carefully enough. He says that I reject SE because Segal has not proven it logically. This is not so. Nowhere do I imply the indefensible idea that a coherent concept must be the conclusion of a logical deduction. What I argue is that Segal's definition of SE does not meet the ordinary standards of reason, for she does not provide clear and well-founded criteria for its application.

He suggests that I am committed to the view that symbolism is reducible to metaphor. But I say nothing of the kind. Rather I make a rough distinction between symbol and metaphor on the basis that the latter always involves resemblance and the former not (always) and go on to suggest that the symbols that are psychoanalytically interesting are those that result from the metaphorical process.

He says that I treat Segal's ‘elementary example’ about violin playing and masturbation as illustrating an inhibition, in which the refusal to play the violin is explained by shameful masturbation wishes. I do not. In fact it is Segal who strongly hints at such an explanation: ‘Prior to his schizophrenic breakdown, the violin had been functioning as a symbol and used for purposes of sublimation. It had only become concretely equated to the penis at the the time of his illness’ (1957: 168).

This paper describes the main themes in the psychotherapy of a severely epileptic girl, over a period of eleven years, aged 16 at the time of writing. For most of the therapy the girl lacked an ability to differentiate between herself and others, and therefore there was little development of rudimentary Oedipal conflicts. Her severe physical and mental impairments were inextricably linked to this fundamental problem in the process of separating: the physical problems compounding the emotional, and the emotional compounding the physical. Her mother's illnesses were significant factors. Throughout the girl's life she was subject to extreme medical interventions. The paper draws upon psychoanalytic models of mind and body integration, including notions of the ‘biopsychosocial dysregulation’ model of illness. The clinical material describes the girl's use of the dolls to populate a Peter Pan Never Land, with its many static perspectives, denying growth and the difference between the generations, although therein was the beginning of the use of symbolization. As the child's awareness of her physical impairments grew, so did her despair at her own and her mother's hopeless physical condition. However, she became more able to express her outrage, but with the life-saving awareness of a therapist who was not also ill. This led to the girl's increased ability to acknowledge differentiation between self and other, further painful awareness of her disabilities, losses and possible death, as well as those of her ill mother and, gradually, an ability to acknowledge the passing of time and an appreciation therein of a healthy separate thinking part of her that could use symbolization and allow for some separateness and some emotional growth.

This paper is based on my experience of working in an outpatient centre for adolescents at risk in a North London borough. The paper focuses on the pressures encountered when adolescent patients want to stop treatment prematurely, and on the risks of re-enactment in the transference. Clinical material is presented from the treatment of an adolescent girl who resorted to cutting herself when she had to face new developmental stages. Finally I attempt to explore how my struggles with letting her go contributed to her psychic development, which has continued since the end of the therapy.

Jenny Kenrick   Consultant Child and Adolescent Psychotherapist. She trained at the Tavistock Clinic and worked for a number of years in multidisciplinary teams in child and adolescent mental health services in south London. She is the assistant organizing tutor for clinical training at the Tavistock Clinic and is co-convenor of the Adoption and Fostering Workshop at the Clinic. Trauma; separation; attachment; nameless dread; continuity of experience; transitional placements.

This paper is concerned with the cumulative nature of the trauma of repeated separations for looked-after children in transitional placements within the care system. Given early experiences of deprivation and abuse and lack of containment both at external and internal levels, these are children who have found themselves alone and unable to process or to attach meaning to experience. Later experience can reactivate earlier catastrophic anxieties.

The description of the three-and-a-half-year psychotherapy of a young child shows how he made use of that therapy to make some sense of his experiences of separation and to form attachments with his therapist and significant care workers. This child's experience in transitional placement is contrasted with that of a child who, in spite of horrific early trauma, benefited from continuity in his care and in his experience of being understood within his family.

The importance of children in transitional placements being given therapeutic help as early as possible, in order to support them in negotiating separation and change on their way to permanent placement, is emphasized.

Roger Kennedy should be congratulated. Dear Editors,

I was interested and delighted to see an article by Frances Thomson-Salo (Vol 26, No. 2 2000) in this journal concerning developments in child psychotherapy in Australia. Having worked in Sydney as a clinical psychologist since 1971 and a child psychotherapist since 1984, I wish to add some further comments, for the situation in Sydney is different from that in Melbourne.

Previous correspondence in the journal (Vol. 25, No. 3 1999) has noted the history of child psychotherapy in Sydney and its difficulties in surviving within a hostile environment. While Sydney is Australia's largest city, with a population of three million people, there are still no designated child psychotherapist positions in the public sector. Moreover there is no psychoanalytic orientation in any undergraduate or postgraduate clinical training in Sydney or the state of New South Wales.

Against this deteriorating trend the Australian Association of Child Psychotherapists was formed in 1985. It consisted of all members of the Association of Child Psychotherapists (UK) who were now living in Australia as well as a small number of child psychoanalysts who were also trained in London. Ms Eve Steel, Dr Averil Earnshaw, Ms Valli Kohon, and myself were on the executive, with five members in Melbourne, five in Sydney, two in Brisbane, and one in Perth and Adelaide. Annual general meetings and national study days were held over the next five years. However the lack of public service positions in child psychotherapy meant that most members were working privately. To survive financially this required seeing more adults and less children. Hence the energy and enthusiasm needed to hold together a federal association was lacking, and while the Australian Association of Child Psychotherapists still exists as a legal entity it has not been functioning since the early 1990s.

This is a description of psychoanalytic consultancy within the social service network around looked-after children. I describe the culture of social services as I have experienced it. I attempt to show how consultancy in various forms can provide an alternative to direct psychotherapy, as well as supporting it, and how it may encourage children and carers to value psychotherapy and even, in some cases, to seek it out for themselves. I demonstrate how it can lead workers to a more positive engagement with the inner world of the children, and with psychodynamic thinking. I explain how my experience has influenced my clinical practice with individual children. I suggest that direct psychotherapy without such consultancy can endanger children's more urgent need for stable placements, and explore some possible reasons. I touch on the need for further training so that as child psychotherapists we can apply our expertise more effectively in this direction.

Group psychoanalytic psychotherapy, ‘work group’ (Bion, 1961), internal parental couple, latency,

In this paper we describe our experience of running a psychoanalytic psychotherapy group for six children, ranging in age from 4-8 years old. The group ran for a year, with sessions held weekly for an hour. The rationale for group work, selection criteria and the treatment setting are discussed. The paper charts the evolution within the children of the concept of an internal ‘work group’ (Bion, 1961), as opposed to a ‘gang’, as their self-awareness and capacity to relate to each other improved. This reflected a corresponding shift in their relationship to the two group leaders, moving from their initial perception of us as neglectful and in conflict with each other, towards recognizing us as a therapist couple who could work together thoughtfully for their benefit. The children's relationship to the group leaders, representing a ‘parental couple’ in the transference, was the focus of much of the work group. The positive outcomes for most of the children, resulting from this treatment, are reported.

This paper explores once-weekly psychotherapy with a 10-year-old boy who had been physically abused and spent six years in various foster-homes before being placed with his birth father and family. This case has many parallels with the experience of late adopted children who may struggle to think about and emotionally digest the experiences of their early lives, while also facing the challenge of joining a new family. This boy's longing for, resentment of and identification with his birth mother were actively communicated through drawings and re-enactments. His expectation of an object as unpredictable and unreliable made it difficult for him to apprehend different experiences with his family and in therapy. Exploring the nature of his internal objects and gradually enabling him to bring feeling and thought into closer proximity provided one way of giving meaning to experiences he could not remember or understand. Technical difficulties in working with a child who actively flaunted the boundaries of the sessions are considered, as is the importance of a containing network surrounding the child.

Jung was the first depth psychologist to propose a concept of the purposive dynamic Self, driving the personality towards its individual destiny, and, although psychoanalysts have since made considerable (unacknowledged) use of concepts of the self and of individuation, it is within analytical psychology that we find the most thorough and long-standing exploration and clinical application of these conceptual tools. Donald Kalsched writes to modify what he sees as Jung's over-optimism about the Self. At its most naive, Jungian theory and practice sometimes seem to take the view that the Self can do no wrong, and that the task of the analyst is simply the creation of a facilitating environment within which the Self can drive forward the individuation process. Kalsched's focus is on the defences which arise in response to trauma, and the difficulties that these pose in the analytic process. He asks why these defences should apparently cause further pathology, and why they should be so intractable and resistant to modification in analysis. These questions are not, of course, in any way new, and have been addressed in some way by virtually every clinician, regardless of school, in writing about analysis.

Kalsched's theoretical contribution is twofold. He suggests that defences which arise in response to severe trauma are archetypal in origin and character; and he terms the process of their creation ‘the self-care system’. It is the impersonal and therefore largely non-negotiable nature of these defences, as they appear clinically, that leads Kalsched to posit an archetypal and hence non-personal root for them. He argues his point succinctly. He states that ‘in trauma, the psyche's goal is survival, not individuation’, and that, when archetypal resources are used to override the individuation processes in favour of survival, the cost to the psyche is the sacrifice of the spirit (p. 66).

Adoption; defects in the object; psychotherapy with adopted children; Oedipus complex; ADHD.

The field of adoption has changed over the past years from one where there were babies available for many adoptive couples to one where increasingly the children who are needing adoption are those who have already suffered deprivations and difficulties in their families of origin, with disrupted attachments and a consequent traumatizing effect of their early history on their internal worlds. Professionals working with these children, who have in effect been ‘dropped’, face the difficult task not only of placing them appropriately but of supporting their adoptive families. With the new experience of a secure base the original trauma may be reworked, and the new framework tested by these damaged and consequently often damaging children as they replay their feelings of being unwanted and unwantable. In describing once-weekly work with a 6-year-old adopted boy, I suggest that the primary disillusion of his neonatal experience caused an internal catastrophe which was then reworked in his adoptive placement. This child did not experience what Winnicott (1971) called ‘gradual disillusion’ in terms of his belief that he creates the needed breast, and thus integration of love and hate of the primary object, but remained in a state of hyper-vigilance because of the deficits in his internal world. These deficits have been able partially to be addressed in psychotherapy treatment.

In Victoria, Australia, children with a history of abuse and severe attachment difficulties, and who have experienced multiple carers and placements, have been traditionally viewed by mental health services as unsuitable for psychoanalytic psychotherapy. A number of factors, including the lack of integrated, long-term case planning; unstable residential placement; and the belief that psycho therapeutic treatment will be of an extended duration, have influenced the decision not to provide individual psychotherapy for these children. Currently, the movement within mental health services is towards responsive and briefer treatment models. The child psychotherapist is challenged to re-think theory, technique and practice. This paper identifies contextual constraints that have led to these children being precluded from accessing psychotherapy. An alternative model of intervention is discussed and illustrated with clinical material. The contributions of Alvarez, Trevarthen, Schore and other writers are drawn on to underpin the clinical work. This model involves a change in technique and role and the use of a time-limited intervention. Intrinsic to the model is the understanding of the child's psycho-biological experience of trauma and disrupted attachment. The child's experiences are conveyed in the pre-verbal, gestural domain to enable history to be given voice.

This paper illustrates how my work has developed over the years and informed my thinking about, and work with, depressed mothers. It also describes the work of the Parent Infant Foundation in Sydney where pregnant women and mothers with infants and toddlers are seen in groups and individually through home visits. The relevance of the support of a peer group when doing such difficult work is described. The paper draws on a central theme: the depressed mother, returning to her own infant beginnings through pregnancy and birth, confronts a dead mother—dead infant dyad. Trauma from the mother's own infancy is seen to have created an internal, autistic, deadened, psychic space. It is argued that behind this deadness lies the primeval pain of abandonment and loss. The associated rage, previously repressed but now awakened by her alive infant and his powerful primitive demands, invade the mother's psyche. The internal deadness freezes her alive processes as mother to her baby. Unbearable pain is awakened — and she may be in terror and unable to move, or she may experience herself as drowning in something catastrophic.

Belief and Imagination rightly and thoroughly embeds psychoanalysis in the wider culture of literature and philosophy. Without claiming for it any special status, Ron Britton explores both what contemporary psychoanalysis can offer to broader discussions about creativity and epistemology and, of equal importance, what it can learn from such discussions. A psychoanalytic text that so fully engages with concepts which underlie the enduring problems of human existence is certainly to be welcomed.

Britton gathers together questions and ideas which he has been formulating, publishing and elaborating over the last decade and a half. Interestingly, although many of the topics were originally written for very different audiences or readerships, they have a distinctive coherence of a kind perhaps recognizable to those who, re-visiting work which may date back many years, discover that they have always been compelled towards the same quandaries and preoccupations. Britton's preoccupations turn out to be with two of the most central and problematic concepts in Western thought, or at least with what place these concepts have in the theory and practice of psychoanalysis and vice versa.

Britton opens the book with some searching questions: ‘What is and where is the Imagination in any modern model of the Mind?’, ‘How can we conceive of it in psychoanalytic terms?’, ‘What is the relationship between belief and knowledge?’ Such questions, of their very nature, have no straightforward answers and Britton, on the whole, explores and suggests rather than asserts. This kind of suggestiveness finds ways of opening up new territory and engendering enthusiasm for further penetration. His challenging interrogatives are interwoven with several other areas of interest.
